newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Moody's rates New York City Euronotes Baa1.
newsitem.headline: Moody's rates New York City Euronotes Baa1.

text.p: Moody's Investors Service said on late Friday it had assigned a Baa1 rating to US$300 million variable rate general obligation Euronotes of New York City.

The rating agency had also confirmed its ratings on the city's other outstanding general obligation bonds, including the Baa1 rating on roughly US$820 million of fixed rate general obligation bonds that were sold recently in the U.S. municipal bond markets.
A state statute authorises New York City to issue up to 10 percent of its general obligation debt as variable or floating rate.
New York City's outstanding variable rate debt amounts to US$3.1 billion, of which about US$1.08 billion is taxable.
Capital investment needs would require substantial additional borrowing, raising the city's already high debt levels, it said.
The current capital plan calls for the issuance of tax-supported debt of about US$3 billion to US$4 billion annually over the next four years, Moody's said.
The city has cut the size of its capital programme by US$2.6 billion through to fiscal 1999 and it would reach the constitutional debt limit earlier than previously planned.

"Under the current calculation of the debt limits, the city projects that total debt subject to the debt limit will be exceeded before the begining of fiscal 1998, if nothing is done," the rating agency said.
Moody's said the chronically late state budget last year had created an ongoing risk to the city's cash flow.

New York City's 12.5 percent personal income tax surcharge, which expired on December 31, 1996, awaits extension by the state legislature although the city has already budgeted revenue from this tax in its current financial plan, Moody's said.

"Persistent out-year gaps and long-term structural imbalance continue to pose a serious challenge to budget stability," the rating agency said. It stressed the city still faced difficult budgetary decisions necessary to cut spending further.
Moody's also noted total employment in the city had declined by about nine percent from the heights of the late 1980s, and well below the peak in the late 1960s.

Employment and economic trends appeared to have stabilised, it said. In particular, strong performance by the securities industry during 1995 and 1996 boosted the city's personal income growth and spending.
"Nevertheless, employment growth in the city is likely to continue to underperform that of the nation," Moody's said.
